Вся диагностика ниже - только МТС. Все три реальных тестировщика (два друга и я сам) оказались на МТС. По МегаФону, Билайну и Т2 — ноль подтверждённых данных, ни в обычном режиме, ни тем более в белых списках. Возможно, часть описанного ниже — не общее свойство белых списков, а специфика конкретно МТС или даже конкретного сегмента их сети

Что подтверждено рабочим

- Обычная DPI-блокировка (не белый список) на МТС — Reality с SNI под популярные домены (vk.com, cloudflare.com) стабильно работает у одного реального пользователя уже несколько недель, тысячи соединений в логах.

Что не работает и не поддаётся объяснению

Второй реальный пользователь, тот же оператор (МТС), но другой сегмент(московский номер, тогда как первый — региональный/южный) — не смог подключиться *ни разу* ни через один из наших серверов (иностранный VPS в Германии, два разных адреса Yandex Cloud), включая периоды, когда белый список точно не был активен (обычный интернет у него при этом работал).

- Пробовали архитектуру с размещением сервера на Yandex Cloud специально ради «коллатерального» прохождения белого списка: зарезервировали статический IP, сверили с публичными списками белых CIDR (community-maintained) — нашли конкретную /22 подсеть внутри /16-пула Yandex Cloud, которая присутствует в таких списках, в отличие от изначально выданного эфемерного адреса (он был из другого /20-пула того же провайдера и в списках отсутствовал). Технически адрес живой — Reality-хендшейк проходит, трафик реально проксируется, проверено с нескольких независимых внешних точек. Но подтверждения работы именно в момент активного белого списка на реальном мобильном устройстве пока нет.
Главная загадка: когда пострадавший пользователь тестирует в момент, похожий на белый список — у него не открывается вообще ничего, включая заведомо белые ресурсы (gosuslugi.ru), которые по логике белого списка должны быть доступны всегда. Это не похоже на учебниковое поведение белого списка (default-deny с проходом только по CIDR+SNI) — скорее на что-то более жёсткое или вообще другую природу блокировки

issues.title: The predictable IP address sequences of one type of GFW DNS injector
issues.body:
> **[§V-B](https://gfw.report/publications/ndss25/en/#5b)** Previous research has shown that the GFW's DNS injection draws fake response IP addresses from a fixed pool—and that different subsets of the pool are used, depending on what name is queried \[[8](https://www.usenix.org/conference/foci20/presentation/anonymous) §3.2\], \[[9](https://www.usenix.net/conference/usenixsecurity21/presentation/hoang) §5.3\]. What has not been appreciated, before now, is that the pools are also *ordered* and *cyclic*. When probed at a high enough rate (around 100 queries per second or more—much greater than an injector's natural injection rate), using a consistent query name and source/destination IP address and port tuple, injected responses repeatedly cycle through IP addresses in the same order (with occasional gaps where the injector responded to queries from other users). By repeated probing, it is possible to get multiple copies of the sequence, reconcile the gaps, and recover the complete ordered list of false IP addresses for a given query name.
>
> ![Figure 8 of Wallbleed, a scatterplot showing the timestamp of DNS responses on the horizontal axis and the reverse-mapped IP address index on the vertical axis. The indices fall into three distinct linear sequences.](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/cf89dd90-7dd2-4a5f-8825-9a68551a3a08)

I want to talk more about this observation made in the Wallbleed paper (#456). Independent of the Wallbleed parsing bugs, the fact that IP address pools of one type of GFW DNS injector are ordered and cyclic is interesting in its own right. I will share some Python programs and give step-by-step instructions on how to run them to see the effect for yourself.

[multiquery.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/19474575/multiquery.zip) (2.4 MB)

* multiquery.py sends DNS queries at a high rate, with the goal of provoking injected DNS responses.
* filter.py isolates responses from the type of injector we are interested in.
* order.py infers an ordering of IP addresses, given a filtered set of DNS responses.
* plot.py draws a graph of IP addresses mapped back to their index in the ordering, revealing linear sequential structure.
* The zip file also includes the CSV data files needed to recreate the analysis below.

### Collect DNS responses

DNS response injection is one of the main mechanisms of network censorship in China. When an ordinary, UDP-based DNS query for a blocked domain name is observed by certain middleboxes at the country's network border, the middlebox sends a forged DNS response back to the DNS client. The forged response contains a fake and useless IP address. Response injection happens even when the destination IP address of the DNS query is not a DNS resolver.

For some domain names, DNS response injection is bidirectional: it responds to DNS queries that are inbound to China as well as outbound. In this demonstration, we'll use the destination IP address 120.52.99.0, which is just an IP address of chinaunicom.com (120.52.99.224) with the last octet set to 0. The blocked domain name we'll use is torproject.org.

Start by collecting a sample of injected DNS responses. About 20,000 queries will be enough. Send the queries at a high rate, 500 queries per second. While the injector is forging responses to our queries, it will also be also forging responses to other naturally occurring queries. By sending at a high rate, we can, for a short time at least, ensure that most of an injector's responses are sent to us, rather than to other DNS clients. We'll also use a fixed source port—keeping the UDP 4-tuple fixed is necessary to ensure that our queries are always handled by the same injector process, as we'll see later on.

Run this command:

```
multiquery.py --num 20000 --rate 500 --qtype A --src-port 10000 --output multiquery-torproject.org-A-srcport-10000.csv 120.52.99.0 torproject.org
```

issues.title: FuzzOverlaySession intermittently misses path lookup callback
issues.body:
## Summary

A long `FuzzOverlaySession` run failed once because the fixture did not observe the expected Core path-notification callback after issuing a validated path lookup. The minimized input passes on replay, so this is an unresolved intermittent failure; it is not yet a confirmed product defect.

## Campaign failure

- yggdrasil-go HEAD: `2c7f050fc5398ecd8ac5f77e9bb5bd91aa2e9e35`
- Go: `go1.27.0 linux/amd64`
- Fuzzer: Go native fuzz engine, `-parallel=2`, runner idle threshold 59 minutes
- `FuzzOverlaySession`: 43,548.6337 seconds, 2,195,558 executions, 203 new interesting inputs, exit 1
- Failure: `overlay_fuzz_test.go:246: validated path lookup did not reach Core callback`
- The input finished in 6.59 seconds against the fixture's 8-second input+cleanup budget; this was not a watchdog timeout or panic.
- Minimized input: `src/core/testdata/fuzz/FuzzOverlaySession/d37961e8216946bd` (SHA-256 `d37961e8216946bd329805bad904b03593a97f3805a82d66bfb917f127e0fb08`).

In `exerciseOverlaySession`, the fixture waits for `SetPathNotify` after sending `SendLookup`. The routing peers and Bloom state have already passed the fixture's readiness checks, and the fixture repeats lookup/maintenance pulses while waiting. The failure may be a routing/callback timing issue or a race in the local test observer.

## Replay evidence

- One seed replay passed.
- 20 replays under `-race` passed.
- A separate 20-run Go execution trace replay passed. The trace bundle is linked in the follow-up issue comment; it is from successful replays, **not** from the original failing execution, which was not reproducible on demand.
- The run used the repository's prepared local Go workspace fixture (`GOWORK` from `tests/ironwood/prepare.py`), not an immutable upstream Ironwood module checkout.
- The fuzz harness and helper sources were untracked in the local checkout at this HEAD; the report does not claim those files are already present on the remote branch.

The trace bundle is linked in the follow-up issue comment because the native issue-artifact upload endpoint returned HTTP 404. It is gzip-compressed/base64-encoded Markdown. Restore it with:

```sh
base64 -d trace.gz.b64 | gzip -d > FuzzOverlaySession-d37961e8216946bd.trace
sha256sum FuzzOverlaySession-d37961e8216946bd.trace
```

Expected raw trace SHA-256: `3320023f487622b30409d970a5e4c0491e94759745d0952d185155d499ce1e3a`.

## Reproduction

The original campaign command was:

```sh
python3 tests/fuzz/run_p0_p1.py local --phase fuzz --until-idle \
  --idle-timeout 59m --jobs 1 --parallel 2 --output OUT
```

Replay the saved seed using the prepared workspace:

```sh
GOWORK=PATH_TO_PREPARED_FIXTURE/go.work \
  go test -tags=ironwood_fuzz,ygg_quic_fuzz ./src/core \
  -run 'FuzzOverlaySession/d37961e8216946bd' -count=20 -timeout=120s
```

The saved seed is currently a campaign artifact. Replaying it is useful for regression checks, but does not reproduce the intermittent failure by itself.

## Request

Please investigate whether this lookup is guaranteed to trigger the Core path callback under these preconditions, and whether the observer/readiness checks provide a synchronized proof of those preconditions. Add a deterministic regression or adjust the harness only after establishing the callback contract. Keep the original failing input and result recorded even if repeated replay continues to pass.

This is potentially related to the routing-convergence discussion in #1409, but reports a distinct `FuzzOverlaySession` callback observation and is not a request to reopen that issue.

When `DisabledComponents` turns IPv6 off on all interfaces (0x01 and 0x10 both set, as in 0xFF), the IPv6 entries of `gateway`, `dns` and `autoSystemRoutingTable` are ignored and the TUN starts with IPv4 only, so the same config works with and without IPv6.

Before the reboot, other programs' IPv6 (TCP, UDP, ping) couldn't leave through Wi-Fi or through an IPv6 adapter added after the TUN started, while IPv4, IPv6 loopback and Xray's own IPv6 still worked. ### Description

On a VLESS + `xtls-rprx-vision` + REALITY server, a client with Mux/XUDP (`concurrency: -1`, `xudpConcurrency: 8`) loses UDP sessions when several of them start at once. The client logs `[Error] common/mux: unknown status: <random number>` (194, 196, ...) or only `[Info] common/mux: failed to read metadata > common/mux: insufficient buffer: 0`. After that, no XUDP session on that mux connection gets any more replies.

Version: v26.10.31, also current `main` (a52db8f6). I think it started in v25.9.5 with 4064f8dd ("XTLS Vision: Refactor code to use DispatchLink() in VLESS inbound").

Replies received, with the configs and scripts below (100 UDP associations opened at once, one datagram each):

| | replies of 100 |
| -- | -- |
| v26.10.31, Vision + XUDP | 88, 60, 79 |
| v26.10.31, Vision + XUDP, server built with `-race` | 40 (17 data race reports on the server) |
| v26.10.31, XUDP without `flow` | 98, 100 |
| v26.10.31, Vision + XUDP, `xudpConcurrency: 1` | 100, 100 |
| `main` with #7337, Vision + XUDP | 100, 100, 99 |

Since 4064f8dd, the VLESS inbound passes its `VisionWriter` to `mux.Server.DispatchLink` directly, with no pipe in between. `mux.ServerWorker` runs `handle()` in a goroutine per session, so several goroutines call `VisionWriter.WriteMultiBuffer` at the same time. `VisionWriter` updates the padding state (`writeOnceUserUUID`, `IsPadding`, `NumberOfPacketToFilter`) without a lock. The client mux then reads the 5-byte padding header as a frame header. The status byte falls on the low byte of the random padding length, which is where the random `unknown status` comes from. `ClientWorker.fetchOutput` exits and takes all sessions of the connection with it.

issues.title: XTLS Vision: Serialize VisionWriter writes from concurrent mux sessions
issues.body:
Fixes #7336

Since 4064f8dd the VLESS inbound hands its `VisionWriter` to `mux.Server.DispatchLink` without a pipe. `mux.ServerWorker` writes from one goroutine per session, so `VisionWriter.WriteMultiBuffer` runs concurrently. The padding state (`writeOnceUserUUID`, `IsPadding`, `NumberOfPacketToFilter`) changes outside any lock, while the `BufferedWriter` lock underneath only covers the socket write. Blocks then reach the wire in a different order from the one their padding was computed in. The client `VisionReader` passes padding through as data, and the client mux fails with `unknown status: <random>`, dropping every session on the connection. Details, configs and logs are in the issue.

This PR makes `VisionWriter.WriteMultiBuffer` hold its own mutex for the whole call, so the padding state and the wire order change together. Mux writes were already serialized by the `BufferedWriter` lock, so throughput stays the same. On plain TCP Vision only one goroutine writes, so the lock is never contended. The same change covers the VLESS reverse portal with Vision, where `mux.ClientWorker` writes from one goroutine per session.

`TestVisionWriterConcurrentWrites` writes to one `VisionWriter` from two goroutines while the underlying writer holds the first write until the second one lands. Without the lock the second block goes out first without the user UUID, and a `VisionReader` on the other side returns padding bytes as payload. The test is deterministic: it fails on `main` without the change and passes with it, with `-race` as well.

The repro from the issue (100 UDP associations at once through Vision + XUDP):

| | replies of 100 | server data races (`-race`) |
| -- | -- | -- |
| v26.10.31 | 88, 60, 79 | 17 |
| this PR | 100, 100, 99 | 0 |

`go test -race ./proxy/ ./common/mux/... ./proxy/vless/...` passes.

issues.title: Inbound: Close and remove the handler when it fails to start
issues.body:
`inbound.Manager.AddHandler` first puts the handler into `taggedHandlers` (or `untaggedHandlers`) and, when the manager is already running, then calls `handler.Start()` and returns its error. Nothing is undone when `Start` fails.

This is the path of `HandlerService.AddInbound` (`xray api adi`). If the new inbound cannot start, for example because one of its ports is already in use, the API returns the error but the handler stays in the manager. Adding it again with the same tag fails with `existing tag found` until it is removed by hand, and the workers that did start (the ports before the busy one in a port range) keep listening.

Now a handler that fails to start is taken out of the manager again and closed, so the ports it opened are released and the tag can be used again. Startup is not affected: handlers from the config are only started later by `Manager.Start`.

Verified with the new `TestAddHandlerFailedStart`, which adds a tagged and an untagged handler whose `Start` fails to a running manager, and then adds the tag again. On main it fails with:

    handler "in" was not closed after failing to start
    handler "in" is still registered after failing to start (1 handlers)

With this change it passes. I also checked it end to end with a dokodemo-door inbound on two ports where the second one was busy: on main the first port stayed bound after the failed add, and adding the inbound again after freeing the port failed with `existing tag found: in`. With the change the first port is free again and the second add works.

Also ran `go test ./app/proxyman/inbound/...` (also with `-race`), `go test ./testing/scenarios -run TestCommander`, `go vet ./app/proxyman/inbound/...`, gofmt and `go run ./infra/vformat/main.go -mode check -pwd ./`.

issues.body:
### Integrity requirements

- [X] I have read all the comments in the issue template and ensured that this issue meet the requirements.
- [X] I confirm that I have read the documentation, understand the meaning of all the configuration items I wrote, and did not pile up seemingly useful options or default values.
- [X] I provided the complete config and logs, rather than just providing the truncated parts based on my own judgment.
- [X] I searched issues and did not find any similar issues.
- [X] The problem can be successfully reproduced in the latest Release

### Description

> 简述：在 v26.10.17（与 main 相同）中，如果 XDRIVE 客户端在下载中途消失（进程被杀或断网），服务端无法察觉：它会继续从目标读取，并把剩余的整个响应写入存储（复现中 20 秒内写入约 235 MiB、607 个对象）。这些对象要等服务端的 mux 子连接自行结束后才会被清理（约 2.7–13 分钟），期间该会话仍被持续 LIST 轮询。原因是 XDRIVE 既没有对端存活检测，也没有背压。

Version: v26.10.17 (`92ccc93`, the newest release and the same commit as current `main`), `network: "xdrive"`, `service: "local"`. XDRIVE is only in the pre-releases since v26.9.30; it is not in v26.3.27. The session logic involved does not depend on the backend, so remote backends behave the same way.

When an XDRIVE client disappears in the middle of a download (process killed, network lost, which is common for mobile clients), the server does not notice:

1. It keeps reading from the target and writes the whole remaining response into the storage. In the repro the client had received 22 MiB of a 256 MiB body; within 20 s after the client was killed the server wrote 246,869,084 bytes in 607 objects.
2. These objects stay until the server-side mux sub-connection ends on its own: about 2.7 min when the target closes the connection after the body, about 13 min with a keep-alive target. Meanwhile the dead session is still polled (about 2 LIST per second).
3. The server logs nothing after the client is gone, even at `debug`.

With a remote backend every abandoned download can upload hundreds of MiB into the storage account, consume API quota and leave the objects there for minutes.

If only the application connection is closed while the client stays alive (curl killed), the server stops writing within about 5 s and the folder is cleaned up, so the problem is specific to the peer disappearing.

| 256 MiB body at 16 MiB/s, `sessionTtlSeconds: 30` | storage at +30 s | +90 s | +180 s | server kept writing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| download completes (control) | 0 B | 0 B | 0 B | no |
| client `kill -9` after ~2 s | 246,869,084 B / 607 objects | same | same | yes, the whole remaining body |
| client `SIGTERM` after ~2 s | 246,394,446 B / 515 objects | same | same | yes |
| curl killed, client alive | 0 B (one `.end`) | 0 B | 0 B | no, stopped within ~5 s |
| client `kill -9`, keep-alive target, watched 900 s | 246,453,796 B | same | same | yes; empty only at ~750–780 s |
| client `kill -9`, target sends `Connection: close` | 246,485,923 B | same | 0 B | yes; empty at ~165 s |

**Cause**

- `Listener.claim` marks the session active (`transport/internet/xdrive/xdrive.go:225`); the mark is removed only in the connection's `onClose` (`xdrive.go:234`). `collect()` skips active sessions (`xdrive.go:267-269`), so the folder of a dead session is not collected while the server-side connection is open.
- That connection is closed only when the inbound handler returns (`app/proxyman/inbound/worker.go:123-127`), i.e. after the server-side mux session ends. XDRIVE has no peer liveness signal: no heartbeat, no idle timeout. `Conn.receive` blocks on the reader channel (`conn.go:53-61`), `walReader.poll` returns quietly on an empty listing (`wal.go:295-297`), `holeTimeout` fires only when later segments exist (`wal.go:312-321`), EOF comes only from a `.end` object (`wal.go:365`).
- No backpressure: `walWriter.Write` appends to the buffer and `flushLocked` starts `go w.upload` (`wal.go:73-91`, `wal.go:127-156`); the semaphore in `upload` limits concurrent `Put`s, not unconsumed data (`wal.go:161-166`). Segments are deleted only by the peer's reader, so nothing limits what

issues.title: Feature Request: Add udp+local:// DNS scheme (plain UDP local mode)
issues.body:
# Feature Request: Add `udp+local://` DNS scheme (plain UDP local mode)

## Summary

Xray's DNS configuration supports `+local` variants for HTTPS, h2c, QUIC and TCP, but there is **no `udp+local` scheme** for plain UDP DNS in local mode. This means there is currently **no way to send plain UDP DNS queries to a local resolver while bypassing the routing/dispatcher stack**.

## Current state

`app/dns/nameserver.go`, `NewServer()` switch (main branch):

```go
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "https"):      // DoH remote
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "h2c"):        // DoH h2c remote
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "https+local"): // DoH local
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "h2c+local"):   // DoH h2c local
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "quic+local"):  // DoQ local
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "tcp"):         // TCP remote
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "tcp+local"):   // TCP local
case strings.EqualFold(u.String(), "fakedns"):
```

Every protocol except plain UDP has a `+local` form. Plain UDP falls through to the default branch:

```go
if dest.Network == net.Network_UDP {
    return NewClassicNameServer(dest, dispatcher, ...)
}
```

Note that `NewClassicNameServer` receives the `dispatcher`, so plain UDP **always goes through the routing stack** — there is no way to bypass it.

## Why this matters (measured data)

For a local resolver (e.g. smartdns on `127.0.0.1`), bypassing the dispatcher matters. Measured on a local resolver over loopback, one A + one AAAA query for the same domain:

| Path | p50 | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `tcp+local://` (current workaround) | ~810µs | 2 TCP handshakes + 2 closes |
| `tcp+local://` pipelined on 1 conn | ~680µs | would need connection pooling, not implemented |
| **plain UDP, 2 packets sent in parallel** | **~376µs** | no handshake, no teardown |

The UDP path is ~2x faster than the current `tcp+local` workaround because it avoids TCP handshake/teardown entirely. Pairing responses by DNS ID worked in 200/200 trials with zero mismatch.

For users running a local caching resolver, this overhead is paid on every cache-miss lookup.

## Secondary issue: port parsing for bare `udp://` schemes

Related bug found while investigating. With:

```json
"dns": { "servers": ["udp://127.0.0.1:5353"] }
```

xray logs:

```
DNS: created UDP client initialized for udp://127.0.0.1:5353:53
```

The port becomes `5353:53` — the `:5353` is swallowed into the address (as a domain string) and then a default `:53` is appended by:

```go
// app/dns/nameserver_udp.go:41
if address.Port == 0 {
    address.Port = net.Port(53)
}
```

This is because `infra/conf/dns.go` builds the endpoint with `Address` and `Port` as separate fields, and `Address.Build()` calls `net.ParseAddress()` on the whole string including `:5353`, while `Port` stays 0.

Attempting `udp://127.0.0.1` (no port) resolves to `udp://127.0.0.1:53`, which happens to work, but the scheme is still parsed as a domain so the connection fails with:

```
failed to open connection to udp:udp://127.0.0.1:53
> too many colons in address
```

Contrast with `tcp+local`, which parses correctly because it uses `url.Hostname()` and `url.Port()` separately (`app/dns/nameserver_tcp.go:75-81`).

## Proposed change

Add a `udp+local` case that mirrors `tcp+local` — parse host/port via `url.Hostname()` / `url.Port()` and pass `nil` as the dispatcher:

```go
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "udp+local"): // DNS-over-UDP Local mode
    return NewUDPNameServer(u, nil, disableCache, serveStale, serveExpiredTTL, clientIP), nil
```

Where the new constructor resolves the destination the same way `baseTCPNameServer` does:

```go
port := net.Port(53)
if url.Port() != "" {
    if port, err = net.PortFromString(url.Port()); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
}
dest := net.UDPDestination(net.ParseAddress(url.Hostname()), port)
```

This would also give users a documented way to hit a local resolver on a non-53 port without the address-swallowing bug.

## Environment

issues.body:
```markdown
Follow-up to #6487, covering the startup-padding part of #6732.

Adds an optional `padding` array to XMC settings with configurable direction per turn:

```json
{
  "padding": [
    {"length": "44", "direction": "c2s"},
    {"length": "64-128", "direction": "s2c"},
    {"length": "25", "direction": "c2s"},
    {"length": "32768-49152", "direction": "s2c"}
  ]
}
```

Each entry specifies a fixed length or inclusive range, plus direction (`"c2s"` for client-to-server or `"s2c"` for server-to-client; full names `"client-to-server"` and `"server-to-client"` are also accepted). Turns can be in any order and direction, including consecutive same-direction turns. Both endpoints need the same array. The first length includes Login Acknowledged's two bytes; invalid ranges and directions are rejected during config loading and connection setup.

Omitting the `padding` field entirely preserves the existing 26.1.2 preset. Custom turns have no intentional delays. Data framing, keep-alives, and mask ordering are unchanged. No new dependency or wire-format change.

This deliberately leaves profile registries, version negotiation, and ongoing traffic scheduling for separate discussion. In particular, existing length checks are not a configuration-fingerprint handshake and do not detect every endpoint mismatch; the documentation calls this out.

Tests cover range validation, direction validation, prefix and VarInt boundaries, default-preset preservation, and encrypted bidirectional round trips with single, odd, and even turn counts.

when you connect to a xray server, the censors can see your TLS ClientHello, read the SNI, and figure out what you are doing and block :)

The RawPacket aka TLS spoofing fixes that by injecting a fake TLS ClientHello before the real one Hits.


The fake one carries like a decoy domain (ex. baidu.com) and then the real one carries your actual destination (ex. www.example.com).

A sensor that captures the first packet sees baidu.com and think that you are just browsing, and everything is okay with that, but in reality your connection goes through :)


It can be configured in the `finalmask.tcp` okay? and its only for client side.


### How everything works


When Xray dials a TCP connection and the first `Write()` happens (which also triggers the real TLS handshake) , our Raw Packet setup does the following.

1.builds a fake Tls ClientHello with whatever SNI you want or you have option to provide the raw bytes (b64).

2.Then we. wrap it in a raw TCP/ip packet.

3.Then deliberately we corrupt the TCP header using whatever method is selected okay?

4. Then we shoot it out via a raw socket

5. Then immediately let the real `Write()` go through normally


In short : two packets arrive at the server back to back and the fake one gets dropped by the servers TCP stack because of the corruption and then the real handshake proceeds like nothing happened.


### Config Example

```json
{
  "streamSettings": {
    "finalmask": {
      "tcp": [
        {
          "type": "rawpacket",
          "settings": {
            "sni": "baidu.com",
            "payload": "",
            "method": "wrong-sequence",
            "ttl": 3,
            "count": 1
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```


### Available Fields

`sni` : The domain to put in the fake ClientHello. If you set this, it will auto generate a valid TLS ClientHello for you automatically. If you set `payload` and `sni` same time , sni wins here.

```
"sni": "baidu.com"
```

`payload` : If you don't want an auto gnrated ClientHello, then just encode your raw bytes that you want into base64 and put them here. I have added an option to do it from command line also. Do like this 

```
 xray tls fake-hello google.com
 ```

It will out the thing and then just copy paste.


Note : If `sni` and payload are empty or not set , the raw packet does nothing and the connection goes through normally.


`method` : It defines how we corrupt the fake packet so the server drops it.

`wrong-sequence` : It duplicates the sequence number (looks like a retransmission so server drops it)

So we grab the kernels `snd_nxt` ( the next sequence number the kernel expects to send), then subtract the length of the fake payload and then use that as the sequence number of the injected packet. The results then is a duplicate of the. last segment, so the receivers TCP stack sees it as a retransmit at best, or like out of window at worst and then drops it.


`wrong-checksum`: It flips all the bits in the TCP checksum (so server sees a bad checksum and drops it)

We build the packet with a correct checksum and then flip every bit(^0xFFFF). The receiver then validates the checksum and its wrong, so the packet goes in trash.

`wrong-ack`: It sets ACK number way outside the receive window (so server sends dup ACK then drops it)

It sets the ACK number to `rcv_nxt - window/2` and that's way outside of the receivers window, and the kernel responds with a dup ACK containing the correct sequence number, then drops it.

`wrong-md5` : This adds a fake TCP MD5 signature option and server without MD5 drops it

Here we append a TCP option with kind=19 and length=18 to the TCP header. The kind 19 is the MD5 signature option (RFC 2385), if the receiver doesn't use TCP MD5 (which is basically everything except some BGP routers), it sees an unknown option

issues.title: XHTTP server: unblock writes and serialize connection close
issues.body:
## Summary

An XHTTP response write can hold the connection mutex while blocked on a slow reader. Closing the logical connection then waits on that mutex, including when a proxy inactivity timeout cancels the business context while the HTTP request stays open.

Signal closure before waiting for the writer and interrupt an active write using `http.ResponseController`. Serialize the complete transition with `sync.Once` so concurrent business/handler closes join the deadline call and the writer before `ServeHTTP` returns.

```text
Close (once)
  signal closure
  interrupt active write
  wait for writer completion
```

## Evidence

- Added `TestConcurrentCloseWaitsForDeadline`, using a real HTTP test server and a gated response writer. The gates ensure the business close owns the first deadline call before the handler closes.
- Upstream implementation: fails with `Close waited for the blocked writer without interrupting it`.
- An unserialized close transition: fails with `deadline call outlived ServeHTTP during concurrent Close`.
- Commit `8628110`, rebuilt with Go 1.27.3 on Linux/amd64: `go test -buildvcs=false ./transport/internet/splithttp -count=1` passes (`ok`, 2.434s).
- Bounded loopback `packet-up` fixtures run against a binary rebuilt from commit `8628110`: peer half-close and an internal inactivity timeout with the HTTP request still open both finish with `CLOSE_FRAMES=0`, `WRITE_FRAMES=0`, and `CLOSE_WAIT_CONNECTIONS=0`.

## Merge Danger

**Door:** Two-way.

**Blast Radius:** XHTTP shutdown. Active I/O is interrupted on close; the existing transport tests cover normal completion.

issues.title: XHTTP: Add configurable error responses
issues.body:
## What

Adds an optional `errorResponse` object to the XHTTP inbound settings, replacing the bare status-only rejections with a service-consistent appearance.

Currently every rejected request is answered with a bare status code: no body, no `Content-Type` (Go's default "404 page not found" or nothing at all). From the terminating side (CDN, reverse proxy, monitoring) a server that answers *every* unknown path with a naked status code and no content type does not look like a normal service.

- `body` and `contentType` apply to every error response the hub writes (404 unknown path, 400/405/409/413/500 etc.), giving all rejections a uniform, service-consistent appearance.
- `statusCode` overrides the status for requests failing the padding validation — the effective authentication gate — allowing 403 semantics instead of the default 400.
- When `errorResponse` is unset, the behavior is unchanged.

Example:

```json
"xhttpSettings": {
  "path": "/api/v2/stream",
  "errorResponse": {
    "statusCode": 403,
    "body": "{\"error\":\"forbidden\"}",
    "contentType": "application/json"
  }
}
```

Resulting surface: unknown paths → `404 {"error":"forbidden"}`, the API gate without valid padding → `403` with the same body — a coherent API host instead of a bare 404/400 machine.

## Notes

- Server-side only. Round-trips through `extra` like the other settings.
- `config.pb.go` regenerated with protoc v6.33.5 / protoc-gen-go v1.36.11 (matches all existing `.pb.go` headers; unmodified proto regenerates byte-identical with this toolchain).
- Proto field `errorResponse = 31` — merges cleanly alongside #7247 (`responseHeaders = 30`); both features are independent.

## Tests

- `Test_WriteErrorResponse`: bare default when unset, configured body + content type, padding-reject status default (400) and override (403).
- `go test ./...` passes locally across all packages, except the pre-existing network-dependent `TestQUICNameServer` in `app/dns`, which fails identically on pristine `main` in my environment (no QUIC egress).

issues.title: XHTTP: Add configurable response headers
issues.body:
## What

Adds an optional `responseHeaders` map (`map<string, string>`) to the XHTTP inbound settings, giving the server control over the headers it writes on responses.

Currently the hub hardcodes a set of response headers: the CORS block for the browser dialer (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`), `X-Accel-Buffering`, `Cache-Control` and the SSE `Content-Type`. With `responseHeaders` an operator can add, override, or remove any of them, as well as set arbitrary extra response headers.

## Semantics

- A key that doesn't collide with a default header is added to every response.
- A key that matches a hardcoded header overrides it.
- An empty value removes that header from the response entirely (including the hardcoded ones).
- When `responseHeaders` is unset, the behavior is byte-identical to before.

Example:

```json
"xhttpSettings": {
  "path": "/api/v2/stream",
  "responseHeaders": {
    "Server": "nginx",
    "Cache-Control": "no-cache, no-transform",
    "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "https://example.com",
    "X-Accel-Buffering": ""
  }
}
```

## Why

- The CORS headers only matter for the browser dialer; a plain server deployment currently emits `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on every response, which is undesirable behind a specific origin and gets flagged by security reviews.
- Reverse-proxy and CDN setups sometimes require specific response headers (`Server`, `Via`, custom headers) or different cache semantics.
- Operators running behind intermediaries may want the response header set to stay consistent with the profile of the service they front, instead of carrying markers that no other service on that endpoint emits.

## Notes

- Server-side only; the client ignores it. It round-trips through `extra` like the other settings.
- `config.pb.go` regenerated with protoc v6.33.5 / protoc-gen-go v1.36.11 — the header matches all existing `.pb.go` files (`check-proto` passes; I verified the unmodified proto regenerates byte-identical with this toolchain first).

## Tests

- `Test_SetResponseHeader`: default / override / removal via empty value.
- `Test_WriteResponseHeader_ResponseHeaders`: CORS default, override, removal, custom header addition, origin echo.
- `go test ./...` passes locally across all packages, except the pre-existing network-dependent `TestQUICNameServer` in `app/dns`, which fails identically on pristine `main` in my environment (no QUIC egress).

issues.title: grpc: close cached clients with their outbound handler
issues.body:
Related to #7177. Requesting review of resource ownership, shutdown semantics, and API compatibility

## Problem

Outbound gRPC clients are cached by destination and MemoryStreamConfig, but core shutdown never closes or removes them. In an embedding process that stays alive, clients can retain connections and continue reconnecting after their core has stopped.

## Change

Give memory stream settings synchronous close-hook registration, and close the resources from their owning outbound handler. Register each ClientConn for exact-entry cache removal and ClientConn.Close. Refuse both reuse and creation after owner closure starts; racing creation must either register for cleanup or close its unpublished client. Cleanup runs outside the settings/cache locks, and concurrent Close callers wait for the same result.

The supported Instance lifecycle is single-start. Each fresh core retains separate ownership even when endpoint and outbound tags match. No per-run generation model, idle-timeout change or per-RPC closure of the shared ClientConn is added.

## Validation

- Synthetic regression reproduces the problem on v26.3.27 and main da2248c.
- `go test -race ./transport/internet ./transport/internet/grpc -count=1 -timeout=120s` passes on this exact branch.
- Official `go run ./infra/vformat/main.go -mode check -pwd ./` passes.
- Tests cover two live cores, sibling streams, normal/MultiMode, fresh-core cycles, failed-start cleanup, multiple destinations, owner/acquisition races, cancellation/backoff and forced dialerProxy lookup contention with Manager.Close.
- Earlier candidate testing also ran the target race suites five times and the dialerProxy test ten times. Those results are supplementary, not a claim that the whole upstream suite passes.

## Review questions / limits

- Handler.Close previously always returned nil. This candidate propagates cleanup errors. Is propagation preferred, or should transport cleanup be logged while preserving the existing return policy? Embedders must distinguish a cleanup error from a still-running core.
- MemoryStreamConfig with resource/mutex state must not be copied; direct external transport callers must close their settings.
- Manager.RemoveHandler still bypasses Handler.Close. XHTTP/nested download settings and TUN eventfd cleanup remain unfixed.
- No general multi-instance guarantee for Xray's other process-global networking state, TLS/Reality/masking matrix, or physical Android packet boundary is claimed.

This is intended as a draft for ownership/API review, not a claim that the Android product defect is resolved.

issues.title: Finalmask: Add the `lua` mask (noise's `script` moves there)
issues.body:
#7174 bolted a second Lua mask onto header-custom, which was the wrong way around. One `lua` mask covers all of it now: it is both a `tcpMasks` and a `udpMasks` entry, and the script decides what it does by the hooks it defines.

-- `HandleHeader(stream, address, role)`, TCP: a free handshake before any traffic, with `stream:Write`, `stream:Read` and `stream:Sleep`. Return a string or an error and the connection is dropped
-- `HandleHeaderWrite(header, address, role)` and `HandleHeaderRead(packet, address, role)`, UDP: prefix every packet with a header, and strip it on the other side by returning its length, or `nil` to drop the packet
-- `HandleNoise(plan, address, role)` is the old noise hook, so `noise`'s `script` is gone (it has not been in a release yet)
-- `role` is `client` or `server`, so one file serves both ends
-- a hook the script does not define is not wrapped at all: a noise only script leaves TCP connections alone and never touches a packet
-- the module is `xray.finalmask` now, with `Random` and `RandomBetween`

```json
{
    "udpMasks": [{"type": "lua", "settings": {"script": "mask.lua", "reset": "30-60"}}]
}
```

Per call it takes at most 64 noise packets and 65535 bytes of noise, 1024 bytes of header, and 65535 bytes each way in a handshake. A packet hook gets 1s, a handshake 30s. A UDP header is one Lua call per packet, the benchmarks in the package cover its cost.

The static lists can follow later, the same script can already do what they do.

issues.body:
# XHTTP: packet-down in stream-down with downlink keep-alive

Follows RPRX's packet-down design in https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/6755#issuecomment-5720463978, which was written while closing the earlier downlink-resume attempt (#6755). That attempt was rejected because "restore connection" is too complex, with latency, ACK and so on. This one does not attempt connection restoration at all. No reconnection, no state machine, nothing to tune: each stream-down GET stays a single request; if the GET dies, the connection dies the ordinary way.

## Problem (from #4846)

CDNs kill a stream-down GET on body inactivity. This matters during uploads: with packet-up the uplink posts keep flowing, but the downlink proxy payload only arrives while the origin sends, so during a pure upload the GET idles and gets cut. Same story for any target that goes quiet for a while after responding.

## What this PR adds

When enabled on both ends, the stream-down response body is cut into packet-down frames with the five elements from the design comment:

- omittable session id excerpt: first 8 bytes of the session id, present on data and keep-alive frames (absent in stream-one where the session id is empty)
- omittable packet seq: uint64, counting data/keep-alive frames per stream-down GET
- mandatory type: data or padding
- mandatory length: uint16
- payload

Use today is the first one from the design comment: downlink keep-alive. While the downlink has been idle for a whole period, the server writes a padding frame (base62, in the spirit of tokenish x-padding) instead of staying silent. Everything the dispatcher sends rides in data frames, which is what lets the client tell padding apart from payload safely; the seq keeps the format ready for the future uses listed in the design comment (retransmission, multi-path-down) without another wire change.

h1, h2 and h3 are covered, since the framers sit on the body, not on a specific transport. stream-one gets the same treatment on its single response body. Browser dialer is out of scope for now: it has no place to read the response header that confirms the framing.

## Negotiation

Strictly opt-in and per request, so old servers are unaffected and nothing breaks behind middleboxes:

1. client config has packetDown: XHTTP stream requests not used as pure uplink (stream-down GET, stream-one request) carry X-Packet-Down: 1
2. server has packetDown configured and sees the marker: it answers with X-Packet-Down: 1 on the response, and frames; without the confirmed header the client never parses frames
3. any other combination: byte-identical wire format as today

## Config

```jsonc
"xhttpSettings": {
  "path": "/sh",
  "packetDown": {              // absent = disabled, as today
    "keepAlive": true,
    "keepAlivePeriod": "10-30",  // seconds; padded when inactive this long. defaults to 10-30
    "keepAliveLength": "24-64"   // padding size. defaults to 24-64
  }
}
```

Server side is the same block in the inbound; the server only honors the feature when the client asks.

## Not in this PR (deliberately)

- obfs of the frames (later, per the design comment)
- retransmission, multi-path-down, same-packet racing, ACK: the format carries seq and the session excerpt, but none of the machinery, exactly like packet-up carries seq today without using it
- nothing about #4846's larger downlink freeze problem (the 15-20 KB per TCP connection cut): this only discards the CDN idle timer, it does not split data across connections

## Tests

- packet_down_test.go: frame round trip (with/without excerpt, with/without seq), byte-stream shaped like a socket, splitting payloads larger than one frame, padding skipped, malformed frame rejected, keep-alive written when idle, keep-alive suppressed while active, config normalization
- splithttp_test.go: full listen/dial round trip with packet-down on both end (100 KiB), and the fallback case with the client setting present but the server without one
- infra/conf: JSON un

issues.title: Outbound: Close the handler when removing it; VLESS Reverse Proxy: Don't start after closing
issues.body:
`outbound.Manager.RemoveHandler`, which `xray api rmo` (`HandlerService.RemoveOutbound`) calls, deletes the handler from the map but never closes it, while `inbound.Manager.RemoveHandler` does. So whatever the removed outbound's `Close()` would release keeps running:

- WireGuard creates its TUN in the constructor (a kernel TUN when available, otherwise a gVisor stack), and once used also has the device with its UDP socket and keepalives.
- VLESS with `reverse` keeps its monitor task: the removed outbound keeps dialing the server every 2 s.
- Same for MASQUE's tunnel. VLESS with `testpre` gets closed too, but its pre-connects only stop reliably with #7113: on main, `Close()` stops just the goroutines waiting to hand over a connection, not the ones redialing an unreachable server.

This shows up wherever outbounds are added and removed at runtime through the API, e.g. by panels.

### Changes

- `RemoveHandler` closes the handler it removed. It does so after releasing the manager lock, so a slow `Close()` (WireGuard) doesn't hold up `Select()`/`GetHandler()` for new connections. Removing an unknown tag still returns nil, and a removed handler is closed only once, since `Manager.Close()` no longer sees it.
- VLESS starts the reverse 2 s after the outbound is created (a goroutine in `New()`), so an outbound removed within those 2 s would still start it after `Close()`. `Reverse.Start()` is now a no-op once `Reverse.Close()` has run.

The other callers of `RemoveHandler` (commander, metrics, reverse portal, VLESS inbound's reverse) remove their own internal outbounds, whose `Close()` is a no-op or idempotent.

Connections already in flight on a removed outbound behave as before unless its `Close()` tears them down (WireGuard, MASQUE). A reverse bridge that is already connected is left to end on its own; only new ones stop.

### Reproduction (on 836a6fe)

Client: `api` with `HandlerService` behind a dokodemo-door inbound, `freedom` as the only configured outbound. Server: a plain TCP listener that only counts accepted connections.

**VLESS `reverse`**: the outbound is added with `xray api ado` and removed with `xray api rmo`. Afterwards `xray api lso` lists only the `freedom` outbound in all runs.

| `rmo` after `ado` | build | accepts at `rmo` | 3 s later | 13 s later |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 7 s | main | 3 | 4 | 9 |
| 7 s | this PR | 3 | 3 | 3 |

issues.title: Bound shutdown after termination signal
issues.body:
This change prevents Xray from waiting indefinitely during graceful shutdown after receiving SIGTERM or interrupt.

Previously, shutdown depended on the deferred server.Close() call returning. If any feature Close() path blocked, the process could stay alive while listeners or active connections continued operating. This made stale Xray processes difficult to detect, especially when another process could bind the same port.

Now Xray runs server.Close() explicitly after receiving a termination signal and waits up to 10 seconds. If shutdown does not complete in time, the process exits with code 1 so supervisors can treat it as a failed shutdown and avoid leaving a functional stale process behind.

This issue was most visible on mobile clients. Some apps, such as Telegram proxy-style traffic, may continue using an already-established path even when the VPN/client UI appears disabled. If the old Xray process remains alive during a stuck shutdown, those connections can continue transferring traffic and updating usage counters, making the node look stopped from the client side while traffic is still flowing server-side.

issues.title: [Feature Request / Proposal] Preventing IP leaks during core restarts / profile switching with autoSystemWfpBlockLeak
issues.body:
Hello Xray-core maintainers and contributors!

First of all, thank you for the recent work on native Windows TUN. Moving leak protection directly into Xray via WFP is a huge step forward and allows GUI clients (like v2rayN) to rely entirely on native Xray TUN rather than legacy multi-core workarounds.

I would like to ask for your thoughts on an architectural edge case related to how GUI clients manage the `xray.exe` lifecycle, and whether addressing it within Xray-core aligns with your vision.

### The Scenario
When a user switches servers, updates routing/DNS profiles, or clicks "Restart Service" in a GUI client like v2rayN, the client terminates the current `xray.exe` process and spawns a new one.

Because the current WFP rules created by `autoSystemWfpBlockLeak` are tied to the dynamic WFP session (`FWPM_SESSION_FLAG_DYNAMIC`) of the running `xray.exe` process, the moment the old process exits, Windows immediately tears down the `xray_tun` adapter and removes the WFP filters. For the ~1–2 seconds it takes for the new `xray.exe` instance to initialize Wintun and re-apply `autoSystemRoutingTable` / `autoSystemWfpBlockLeak`, the OS falls back to the physical interface (direct), causing a brief IP/traffic leak.

### Possible Approaches
I am wondering what the maintainers think about bridging this restart gap natively in Xray. A couple of concepts come to mind:

1. **CLI-Managed / Companion WFP Lock:**
   Adding an optional flag or lightweight CLI subcommand (e.g., `xray tun-wfp lock` / `unlock`, or a helper mode bound to the parent GUI PID so it still utilizes `FWPM_SESSION_FLAG_DYNAMIC` for crash safety) that holds the baseline `"all"` / `"allexceptlan"` WFP block rules across worker restarts. This way, a GUI client could arm the WFP filter once when starting its session, restart `xray.exe` processes freely without dropping the WFP wall during the 1–2s gap, and disarm it on deliberate exit.

2. **Graceful Config Reloading for TUN:**
   While Xray already has gRPC APIs for dynamic outbound/routing updates, full profile switches in GUI clients often rewrite the entire config. Allowing `xray.exe` to reload its configuration on the fly (via API or signal) without destroying the active `wintun` adapter and its dynamic WFP session would eliminate both the Wintun recreation delay and the leak window.

### Question to Maintainers
How do you view this problem from Xray's design perspective?
1. Do you think bridging this restart gap belongs with in Xray-core, or do you consider it strictly the responsibility of external GUI clients?
2. If addressing it in Xray-core makes sense to you, what architectural direction would you prefer (one of the concepts above, or a completely different approach)?

If this aligns with the project's goals, I might be open to exploring the codebase further and perhaps drafting a PR for your review.

Thank you for your time!

### 描述

这个问题比较严重，很多Claude用户被封可能和这个issue有关

使用vless enc+xhttp+vision过Cloudflare ECH alpn=h3节点（用<https://github.com/Anthrop44/3x-setup>一键部署的），客户端为Linux v2rayN，使用Xray TUN和域名分流。在访问 openai.com 时被阻止访问并提示`Country, region, or territory not supported`而且被显示真实ip了。于是意识到有部分流量没有经过代理出口。切换到同一代理服务器的直连节点vless+xhttp+tls后访问恢复

<details>
<summary>GPT分析的</summary>
### 原始部署与最小复现的关系

已通过只读SSH读取生产服务器正在使用的`/usr/local/x-ui/bin/config.json`和`/etc/caddy/Caddyfile`，并核对服务端版本。没有修改或重启生产服务

| 生产节点 | VLESS Encryption | flow | 公网传输 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Direct h2/h3 | `encryption/decryption=none` | 无Vision | XHTTP + TLS，h2或h3 |
| Cloudflare ECH h2/h3 | `mlkem768x25519plus.xorpub`，客户端`0rtt`，服务端`600s` | `xtls-rprx-vision` | XHTTP + TLS/ECH，h2或h3 |

生产架构：

```text
Direct客户端 -> Caddy:443 -> h2c -> Xray Direct入站:8084
CDN客户端 -> Cloudflare边缘:443 -> Caddy回源监听 -> h2c -> Xray ENC+Vision入站:8087
```

所以从Cloudflare ECH h3切换到Direct h2同时改变了CDN路径、VLESS Encryption、Vision和ALPN，不能把恢复简单归因于h3变成h2。生产Xray的两个XHTTP入站均为`security=none`，TLS由Caddy/Cloudflare处理；这不代表公网传输没有TLS

最初曾用普通VLESS（`encryption=none`）+ RAW + TLS + Vision做本机最小复现，成功观察到同样的后续包direct现象。为了覆盖实际使用的VLESS ENC方案，本报告已追加并以**VLESS Encryption + XHTTP + TLS + Vision、ALPN h3**作为主要本机复现，且完成h2及flow对照

### 受控对照结果

下面各组使用相同的本机VLESS ENC密钥对、测试UUID、XHTTP路径、域名分流和默认direct规则。服务端仅监听回环地址，不经过Cloudflare或Caddy。每组发起两次相同curl HTTP/3请求，分别控制节点传输ALPN及客户端/服务端flow

注意两个不同层次：表中h2/h3是**客户端Xray到代理服务器的外层XHTTP传输**；测试应用curl始终使用HTTP/3，即内层UDP/443

| 外层ALPN | 客户端flow | Vision拒绝次数 | 客户端proxy记录 | 客户端direct记录 | UDP接收器收到包数 | 路径判断 |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| h2 | `xtls-rprx-vision` | 4 | 4 | 2 | 2 | 拒绝后由客户端直连 |
| h3 | `xtls-rprx-vision` | 4 | 4 | 2 | 2 | 拒绝后由客户端直连 |
| h2 | `空（服务端同步不启用Vision）` | 0 | 2 | 0 | 10 | 客户端保持proxy，服务端转发 |
| h3 | `空（服务端同步不启用Vision）` | 0 | 2 | 0 | 10 | 客户端保持proxy，服务端转发 |
| h2 | `xtls-rprx-vision-udp443` | 0 | 2 | 0 | 10 | 客户端保持proxy，服务端转发 |
| h3 | `xtls-rprx-vision-udp443` | 0 | 2 | 0 | 10 | 客户端保持proxy，服务端转发 |

接收器和代理服务器都在同一台机器，所以“收到UDP包”本身不等于泄漏。路径判断同时核对客户端路由日志和服务端转发日志：普通Vision组的包由客户端direct发出；空flow及`-udp443`组的包由代理服务器转发，客户端没有direct记录。接收器不提供HTTP/3服务，所以各组curl最终都超时，不能以curl超时与否判断路径

实验说明：

- VLESS ENC+Vision在外层h2、h3下均复现，不是h3特有问题
- 普通VLESS+TLS+Vision也复现，所以VLESS Encryption不是必要条件
- 完全移除Cloudflare/ECH后仍复现，所以不能把问题限定为Cloudflare CDN或ECH故障
- 仅保留ENC、去掉Vision后，h2/h3两组没有出现该拒绝及后续direct路径

The data in #6268 and #7099 comes from phone clients. This is a different case: tunnels between nodes. One node dials two others as an XHTTP client (`stream-one` + REALITY), with one stream per proxied connection, about 8000–11000 concurrent. Environment: 8 GB VM, no swap, Go 1.27.3, an Xray fork that includes this PR.

**Before:** xray was OOM-killed 4 times in about 27 hours (anon-rss 6.4–7.2 GiB). 99.6% of sampled heap came from `http2.(*clientStream).writeRequestBody`, each object exactly 524288 bytes.

**Change:** only `"h2Params": {"MaxReadFrameSize": 16384}` on the server inbounds; the client config is unchanged.

**Two runs from a cold start, similar uptime and load (about 57700 goroutines):**

| MiB | Before (135 s) | After (144 s) |
|---|---|---|
| RSS | 3172 | 1867 |
| HeapAlloc | 5371 | 901 |
| Sys | 7473 | 1969 |
| NextGC | 9984 | 1473 |

At 12 min 26 s of process uptime, RSS was 4445 and 2188 MiB. The changed setup has only run for about 12 minutes so far, with no OOM yet; the longest run before the change lasted 24 h 36 min, so it is too early to say the OOM kills are gone.

**Loopback test** (same binary, no RTT or loss, 1000 streams, 5 interleaved rounds, before / after): upload on 1 stream 1747 / 1756 Mbit/s, on 8 streams 3439 / 3816 Mbit/s, download 1426 / 1433 Mbit/s; no slowdown seen. After 8 rounds of opening and closing streams, RSS was 311–336 / 139–146 MiB.

comments.issue_title: XHTTP server: Add `h2Params`
comments.body:
In `ListenXH`, `h2Params` is parsed after the TCP/Unix listener has already been opened. If `json.Unmarshal` fails, the function returns `nil, error` without closing that listener.

For example, this happens with `"h2Params": []`. The caller receives no listener to close, so the port may remain occupied after startup fails, preventing a subsequent start on the same port within the same process.

I suggest adding `_ = l.listener.Close()` in `transport/internet/splithttp/hub.go`, before the existing return of the `failed to parse HTTP2Config` error. This would release the acquired resource while preserving successful startup behavior and the existing error for invalid configurations.

issues.title: Возможность распределения трафика по нескольким туннелям
issues.body:
Просьба рассмотреть возможность создания нескольких параллельных туннелей, но в рамках одного VPN интерфейса.

Сейчас для VLESS протокола трафик идет на один сервер с одним IP.

Это, как бы так сказать, не очень хорошая идея. Сторонний наблюдатель банально по распределению статистики трафика между пользователем и сочетанием IP - SNI может вычислить, что подключения к этому IP с этим SNI - c 99% являются VPN туннелем, даже если вы используете Reality и это выглядит как трафик с настоящего сайта.

Как это можно исправить: поднимать несколько параллельных туннелей и заворачивать трафик в них, с периодической ротацией пула одновременно активных туннелей и случайным распределением не самого трафика, а балансировки нагрузки между туннелями. Это намного более естественный паттерн, который сложно вычислить.

Возможные минусы и проблемы: для корректной работы сайтов нужно, чтобы в пуле одновременно используемых соединений, точка выхода (IP, с которых трафик идет уже на сами сайты) была одной и той же. Это поможет избежать блокировок уже со стороны самих сайтов, т.к. постоянная смена IP может быть воспринята как DDOS или какая-то другая атака. Так как Free и Premium сервера целиком под вашем контролем, маршрутизация с разных точек входа на одну точку выхода не выглядит как неосуществимая задача. У этого решения есть своя цена: вероятность обнаружения точек входа снижается, но при обнаружении они отвалятся все пачкой. Поэтому прежде чем это делать, необходимо убедиться в отсутствии уязвимостей, выдающих точки входа.

Если это невозможно и все используемые серверы имеют разные выходные IP (сторонние подписки и Self-Hosted решения) - сегментировать исходящий трафик по GeoIP целевых сайтов, куда идёт обращение, таким образом чтобы допустим на сайты в Германии трафик шел через туннель A, на сайты США - через туннель B. Случайного распределения балансировки тут уже не выйдет, но даже в таком случае оно уже не будет выглядеть как весь трафик в одну точку.

issues.title: fix: handle dual-stack WireGuard addresses and IPv6 endpoints
issues.body:
WireGuard/AmneziaWG profiles containing both IPv4 and IPv6 interface addresses are passed to the desktop daemon as a single IPv4 address. On macOS this fails with `Failed to set IPv4: Destination address required`. Resolved IPv6 server addresses are also assigned to IPv4 fields, and the macOS backend emits an unbracketed IPv6 endpoint, failing with IPC error -22.

The iOS/macOS Network Extension has a separate config serializer which also emits IPv6 endpoints without brackets, causing WireGuardKit to reject the generated config before starting the tunnel.

This change:

issues.body:
## Feature request

I want to enter a domain once and have it continue following the selected split-tunneling policy when its IP addresses change, without editing the list or reconnecting the VPN. I also want rules such as `*.example.com` for subdomains.

A domain should remain the rule's identity. Addresses resolved when it was added or at connection time must not become a permanent substitute for that rule.

My immediate use case is Windows with WireGuard/AmneziaWG, in both sites-only and all-sites-except-listed modes.

## Expected behavior

- An exact rule such as `example.com` follows changes to that hostname's DNS addresses during an active session.
- A wildcard rule such as `*.example.com` matches real queried subdomains, including nested ones, without enumerating them in advance.
- Proposed wildcard semantics: match `api.example.com` and `a.b.example.com`, not `example.com`, `notexample.com` or `example.com.evil.test`. Add the apex separately when needed.
- Handle multiple addresses and CNAME chains, and keep mappings/routes current with DNS lifetime and network changes.
- Establish the selected routing policy before the application uses a newly resolved address, without restarting the tunnel or disrupting unrelated connections.
- Preserve literal IP/CIDR rules, local hosts mappings and import/export of the domain or mask itself.
- Show resolution/application failures instead of silently presenting a stale rule as current.

A wildcard is a routing-rule pattern, not a request to resolve the literal hostname `*.example.com`. It also does not automatically include unrelated CDN domains used by a page.

## Acceptance scenarios

1. Add an exact domain whose DNS answer initially points to address A.
2. Keep the VPN connected, change the answer to B, and let the previous DNS answer expire.
3. A new connection to that domain must follow the same configured policy through B, without deleting/re-adding the rule or reconnecting.
4. Add `*.example.com`, then request a previously unseen subdomain. The first connection after its DNS response must follow the wildcard rule.
5. Repeat for both site-routing modes, multiple DNS answers, CNAME targets, temporary DNS failures, changed networks and rule removal.
6. Verify that a shared address is not removed while another rule still needs it, and define safe handling of cached answers and existing connections.

These are acceptance requirements. The implementation PR below documents which scenarios are covered by isolated tests and which still require on-device verification.

## Design constraints

A local DNS handler is a possible foundation, but simply periodically resolving known hostnames is insufficient for previously unseen wildcard subdomains.

DNS-to-IP routes also have a shared-IP limitation: unrelated hostnames on the same address cannot be distinguished by an ordinary IP route. The design must explicitly distinguish dynamic IP-based exclusions from strict per-domain connection routing; stronger isolation may need a domain-aware traffic path.

Applications using their own encrypted DNS can bypass a local DNS handler. Do not silently disable browser Secure DNS/DoH or intercept/decrypt HTTPS. Document supported DNS paths and any required opt-in configuration. IPv6 support or limitations must also be explicit, rather than letting AAAA traffic silently ignore the rule.

DNS updates must respect the chosen direct/tunnel resolver policy and must not introduce unintended DNS leaks.

## Related work

- #1217 asks the same underlying question about changed IPs in Windows exclusions.
- #1423 is the broader site-split-tunneling feature tracker; its [DNS-refresh discussion](https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/issues/1423#issuecomment-5131614693) overlaps this request.
- #3376 / #3380 address normalization and refresh before connection/reconnection. They do not implement continuous live updates or wildcard discovery.
- Project tracker: #3378.

Fixes #3377.

I encountered exclusions remaining visible in settings while their destinations still used the tunnel, and slow/intermittent connectivity with a large exclusion list.

issues.body:
## Summary
Adds a ping tester and a live speed meter.
- **Server list:** every server shows its latency (for example `48 ms`) and a quality badge: Excellent, Good, Fair or Poor. A red **Unreachable** badge appears when a TCP-based server does not accept connections. A neutral **No reply** badge appears when a UDP server ignores every probe. All servers are tested when the list opens, and a refresh button sits next to the "Servers" header.
- **Home screen:** ping and quality of the current server. While connected, it also shows the tunnel's live download and upload rate, updated every second.
It only needs the host and port from each server's config: no SSH and no gateway calls. So it works for self-hosted servers, Amnezia Premium/Free and imported configs (WireGuard/AmneziaWG, OpenVPN, Xray VLESS/VMess/Trojan/Shadowsocks). Probes go straight from the device to the server's own endpoint, and no addresses are logged.
## How it works
**Latency:** `core/utils/latencyProbe` sends 4 samples 200 ms apart, each with a 1.5 s timeout.
- **TCP-based configs** (OpenVPN over TCP, Xray): measures the TCP handshake time to the server port.
- **UDP-based configs** (WireGuard/AWG, OpenVPN over UDP): sends ICMP echo through the existing Mozilla `PingSender`s.
  - If ICMP gets no answer, it falls back to a TCP handshake to the VPN port. Amnezia's own `setup_host_firewall.sh` drops echo requests, so this is common.
  - In the fallback, a refusal (RST) counts as an answer, since it proves the host is up.
- **Handshake implementation:** a native non-blocking `connect()` watched by a `QSocketNotifier`. `QTcpSocket` can't set socket options before it connects, and Windows needs SYN retransmissions turned off (`SIO_TCP_INITIAL_RTO`). Otherwise Windows retries a refused SYN for about a second, the answer misses the timeout, and a working server shows as unreachable.
- **Quality:** under 80 ms is Excellent, under 150 Good, under 300 Fair, anything else Poor. The result drops one step on packet loss or jitter above 50 ms.
**Controllers and model:**
- `core/controllers/serverLatencyController` extracts each server's endpoint, runs the probes and keeps the results.
- While connected, it re-tests only the current server, because other servers would be measured through the tunnel.
- `ServersModel` gets `latencyMs`, `latencyQuality` and `isLatencyTesting` roles.
- `ServerLatencyUiController` exposes the current server's result and the testing state to QML.
**Speed:** computed once per second on the VPN thread from counters that already exist, so it adds no traffic.
- **OpenVPN:** the management interface's `bytecount`.
- **WireGuard/AWG and Xray on Windows, Linux and macOS:** byte counters of the tunnel interface (`GetIfEntry2`, sysfs, `NET_RT_IFLIST2`).
- **iOS and macOS Network Extension:** WireGuard runtime stats; Xray uses `hev_socks5_tunnel_stats`.
- **Android:** the service's `STATISTICS_UPDATE` events.
- **No counter available** (for example IKEv2 on Windows): the speed row is hidden.
**Build changes:**
- `cmake/sources.cmake`: the client now builds `mozilla/pingsender*` and the platform ping senders.
- `windowspingsender.cpp`: `char8_t` changed to `uint8_t` so it compiles in the C++17 client. Until now only the C++20 service built it.
- `tests/CMakeLists.txt`: `mozilla/pingsenderfactory.cpp` gets its `MZ_<PLATFORM>` define in test builds, because it fails with `#error` without one.

issues.title: windows: add split tunnelling exclusion routes in one batch
issues.body:
## Problem

On Windows, "all sites except" split tunnelling with a large site list makes
activation take minutes. The daemon installs one exclusion route per listed
prefix, and each one re-reads the whole, growing, routing table. With about
8,700 prefixes, 5.1.0.6 took almost 5 minutes from `activate` to
`Connection status: 1`.

This PR fixes that slow route install, and only that. A separate issue
remains after activation: the GUI can stay on "Connecting..." for minutes
more, because the daemon's 250 ms `checkHandshake()` timer is starved while
`routeChanged()` rescans run on the same thread. This PR does not change
that path; see Known limitations.

## Observed symptom

- AmneziaVPN 5.1.0.6 on Windows 10 22H2, AmneziaWG, "all sites except" mode
  with a Russian-IP bypass list: about 8,700 IPv4 prefixes (8,675 exclusion
  route add attempts in the run below).
- In the service log, 4 min 57 s pass between `Command received: activate`
  and `Connection status: 1`, with 30,428 `WindowsRouteMonitor` lines in
  between, almost all of them from adding exclusion routes one by one.
- The reporter also found that installing the same routes from a script
  (`netsh -f`, 500 commands per batch) is fast. That timing is not included
  here. It suggests, but does not prove, that creating the routes is not the
  bottleneck. The counts below locate the cost.

## Root cause

In this mode every listed site becomes an entry in `excludedAddresses`, and
`Daemon::activate()` (and `Daemon::switchServer()`) call
`addExclusionRoute()` once per address. On Windows,
`WindowsRouteMonitor::addExclusionRoute()` does the following for **every**
prefix:

1. `GetIpForwardTable2()`: copies the whole routing table out of the kernel.
   The table grows by one row for each exclusion route already added.
2. `updateInterfaceMetrics()`: calls `GetIpInterfaceTable()` and writes one
   debug line per connected interface.
3. `updateCapturedRoutes(family, table)`: when default route capture is on,
   this calls `isRouteExcluded()`, which is linear in the number of
   exclusions, for every eligible system route.
4. `updateExclusionRoute()`: a linear scan of the table.
5. One more debug line.

Every log line is flushed to the log file. For N prefixes the cost is O(N²)
table rows copied out of the kernel and scanned. During `switchServer()`,
where capture is already enabled, it adds O(T·N²) in `isRouteExcluded()`,
where T is the number of system routes. For N = 8,664 that is about
37 million rows copied (see the measurements below).

## Fix

- Add `WindowsRouteMonitor::addExclusionRoutes(const QList<IPAddress>&)`. For
  each address family it fetches the routing table and interface metrics
  once, then builds each exclusion row, computes its next hop against that
  snapshot with the existing `updateExclusionRoute()`, installs it, and
  records it in `m_exclusionRoutes`. `updateCapturedRoutes()` runs once at
  the end. A single summary line (`Added X of N exclusion routes (I
  installed, F failed) in T ms`) replaces the per-prefix debug lines.
  Interface, capture, warning and error lines are logged as before, but
  `updateInterfaceMetrics()` now runs once per family.
- `addExclusionRoute()` keeps its signature, its log line and its return
  value, and now calls the batch with one prefix. The row initialisation
  moved verbatim into `initExclusionRow()`.
- `updateExclusionRoute()` now returns `false` when `CreateIpForwardEntry2()`
  fails. It still logs the error as before. The batch uses the value only
  for the summary count, and `routeChanged()` ignores it.
- `WireguardUtils` gets a virtual `addExclusionRoutes()` whose default adds
  the routes one by one, so Linux and macOS routing code is unchanged.
  Windows overrides it, and `excludeLocalNetworks()` uses it too. The
  daemon-level duplicate handling below applies to every platform.
- `Daemon::addExclusionRoute()` is replaced by `Daemon::addExclusionRoutes()`.
  It applies the same `m_excludedAddrSet` reference counti

issues.title: Deadlock between AmneziaVPN-service and kernel network locks on lid close (macOS 26.6, app 5.0.0.5, VLESS) — configd killed by WATCHDOG
issues.body:
## Summary

On macOS 26.6 (25G72), closing the MacBook lid while the VPN is connected reliably
deadlocks the system networking stack. A kernel lock cycle forms between
`AmneziaVPN-service` and the kernel, `configd`'s `IPConfigurationAgentQueue` stalls,
and after 60 seconds the watchdog terminates `configd`.

This happens every single day, on every lid close with the VPN running.

## Environment

- AmneziaVPN for macOS **5.0.0.5**
- macOS 26.6 (build 25G72)
- MacBookPro18,3 (Apple Silicon)
- Protocol: **VLESS (XRay)**
- `tun2socks` is present in the process list (41 threads), consistent with the
  XRay/VLESS userspace tunnel path
- Report incident ID: 19D61D4C-C90C-4BF8-AE79-91B9C65CAC96
- Report type: bug_type 409 (WATCHDOG stackshot), `displayState: OFF`

## Steps to reproduce

1. Connect the VPN.
2. Close the MacBook lid.
3. Within ~60 seconds a `configd` watchdog report is generated.

## Actual result

`configd` is killed by the [watchdog]

## Root cause from the stackshot — four-way lock cycle

1. `configd` thread 103010 (`IPConfigurationAgentQueue`) waits on kernel mutex
   `0xfffffe000c571830`, owned by kernel thread 103456 (`thread call high #27`).
2. Kernel thread 103456 waits on krwlock `0xfffffe000c5a4270` **for reading**,
   owned by thread 104354.
3. Thread 104354 belongs to **AmneziaVPN-service (pid 553)** and waits on kernel
   mutex `0x5162d882b476c1c1`, owned by kernel thread 5256.
4. Kernel thread 5256 waits on mutex `0xfffffe000c571830` — back to 103456.

The cycle never breaks, so the whole networking subsystem stalls.

## Additional observations

- `AmneziaVPN-service` had **259 threads** and **~955 MB** resident memory, with
  ~592k page faults. Roughly 200 of those threads were parked on the same
  `0xfffffe000c571830` mutex, and about a dozen more on the krwlock held by 104354.
  The thread and memory growth looks like a leak independent of the deadlock.
- `tun2socks` (41 threads) is blocked on the same mutex.
- The `AmneziaVPN` GUI process is also stuck: thread 16371 waits on krwlock
  `0xfffffe000c5a4270` for writing, owned by 104354.

## Likely trigger

On lid close macOS tears down Wi-Fi and reconfigures interfaces, so `configd`
dismantles network services while the client simultaneously tears down its `utun`.
The two sides appear to acquire the network locks in opposite order.

## Workaround

Disconnecting the VPN before closing the lid avoids the issue entirely.

## Attachment

Full watchdog stackshot attached.

[Error.rtf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30687946/Error.rtf)

# macOS: Site-based split tunneling is not applied for AWG/WireGuard — always full tunnel

## Environment

- AmneziaVPN client: **5.0.3.0** (macOS pkg, universal)
- OS: **macOS 27.0.1** (Apple Silicon, arm64)
- Protocol: **AWG** (self-hosted server, amneziawg-tools v3.1.20260812)
- GUI state: Settings → Split tunneling → Sites → **"Only for selected sites"** (`Conf.routeMode = 1`, `Conf.ForwardSites` populated with 36 domains), VPN reconnected after the change

## Summary

On macOS, for AWG (and WireGuard) connections, the site-based split tunneling settings are **silently ignored** — the connection is always full tunnel. Two independent code paths cause this:

### 1. Route-split logic is skipped for AWG/WG containers

`client/vpnConnection.cpp` (`VpnConnection::onConnectionStateChanged`, Connected branch) wraps the **entire** split-tunneling route logic in:

```cpp
// line 135
if (!ContainerUtils::isAwgContainer(container) && container != DockerContainer::WireGuard) {
    ...
    if (m_appSettingsRepository->isSitesSplitTunnelingEnabled()) {
        // routeDeleteList("0.0.0.0"), VpnOnlyForwardSites -> addSitesRoutes(),
        // VpnAllExceptSites -> 0.0.0.0/1 + 128.0.0.0/1 ...
    }
}
```

For AWG and WireGuard containers none of this ever runs: neither forward-site routes (include mode) nor exception routes (exclude mode) are added, and the DNS servers are not excluded from the tunnel on macOS.

### 2. Client config is hardcoded to full tunnel

`client/core/configurators/wireguardConfigurator.cpp` (line 275):

```cpp
clientConfig.allowedIps = QStringList { "0.0.0.0/0", "::/0" };
```

This is unconditional — the configured split-tunneling mode is not reflected in `AllowedIPs`. The macOS daemon then expands the default route into two halves (`client/platforms/macos/daemon/wireguardutilsmacos.cpp`, `updateRoutePrefix`, line 357):

```cpp
return m_rtmonitor->insertRoute(IPAddress("0.0.0.0/1")) &&
       m_rtmonitor->insertRoute(IPAddress("128.0.0.0/1"));
```

So every AWG connection gets `0/1` + `128.0/1` → tunnel, i.e. full tunnel, regardless of GUI state.

### 3. Related: `routeGateway()` is never set for WG/AWG

`VpnProtocol::routeGateway()` is only populated by the OpenVPN (`openVpnProtocol.cpp:172,178`) and Xray (`xrayProtocol.cpp:33`) protocols. For WireGuard/AWG it stays empty. The macOS-only branch in the `VpnAllExceptSites` path relies on it:

```cpp
#ifdef Q_OS_MACOS
    iface->routeAddList(m_vpnProtocol->routeGateway(), QStringList() << dns1 << dns2);
#endif
    addSitesRoutes(m_vpnProtocol->routeGateway(), routeMode);
```

— so even for protocols where the split logic runs, on macOS the DNS exclusion routes and site routes are added via an **empty gateway** whenever the protocol is WG/AWG (`routeAddList("", ip)` silently fails).

## Steps to reproduce

1. macOS 27.0.1 (arm64), AmneziaVPN 5.0.3.0, self-hosted AWG server
2. Settings → Split tunneling → Sites → mode "Only for selected sites", add e.g. `youtube.com`
3. Connect via AWG
4. `route -n get alfabank.ru` (not in the list) → `interface: utunX` (tunnel) — expected `en0`
5. `route -n get youtube.com` → `interface: utunX` — this one is correct, but only because everything is routed into the tunnel

## Actual result

- `route -n get default` → en0, but `0/1` + `128.0/1` → utun (full tunnel in practice)
- Sites **not** in the forward list (including the configured DNS servers, e.g. 1.1.1.1) are routed through the tunnel
- GUI split-tunneling settings have **no effect** on AWG connections

## Impact

- "All except sites" mode cannot keep RU-local resources (banks, gov services) on the direct path — they egress via the VPN IP
- Overlay VPNs that must coexist with Amnezia (e.g. Tailscale system extension) break under the captured routes: their control-plane sockets and UDP (STUN/DERP) die, `tailscale netcheck` reports `UDP: false`, controlplane unreachable — while ordinary user processes through the tunnel work fine
